column9: stem
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Which description best fits a karyotype?
column14: A family tree that tracks one trait through many generations of the same family
column15: A grid used to predict the genotypes of offspring
column16: An organized picture of a cell's chromosomes, sorted into pairs by size
column17: A list of every DNA base in a single gene
column28: A karyotype is a picture of a cell's chromosomes arranged in matching pairs from largest to smallest. A family tree is a pedigree and the prediction grid is a Punnett square; mixing these three tools up is the most common mistake because all of them are used to study inheritance.
column29: Karyo- means nucleus. Which choice is a picture of what is inside the nucleus?

column9: How many chromosomes are in a typical human body cell, as shown on a karyotype?
column28: A typical human body cell has 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Answering 23 counts pairs instead of chromosomes (or gives the number in an egg or sperm), and 44 counts only the autosomes.
column29: Count single chromosomes, not pairs. Each pair has two.

column9: How many pairs of autosomes does a typical human karyotype have? Type a number.
column28: Pairs 1 through 22 are autosomes, so there are 22 pairs. The 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes (XX or XY), so answering 23 is the common mistake.
column29: One pair on the karyotype is not an autosome pair. Which one?

column9: How are the chromosome pairs numbered on a human karyotype?
column15: From largest (pair 1) to smallest (pair 22)
column16: In the order the chromosomes appeared in the photo
column17: Alphabetically by the genes they carry
column28: Autosome pairs are numbered by size, with pair 1 the largest and the numbers going up as the chromosomes get smaller. Students often flip this and think pair 1 is the smallest.
column29: Think about how the very first pair on a karyotype compares in size to the rest.

column9: Pair 23 on a karyotype shows two X chromosomes. What is the person's biological sex?
column15: Male
column16: It cannot be told from a karyotype
column17: Female
column28: XX is female and XY is male. A karyotype is one of the clearest ways to see biological sex, so saying it cannot be told is a mistake. Klinefelter syndrome needs a Y as well (XXY).
column29: Which sex chromosome would a male have that is not in this pair?

column9: Chromosome pair 23, which is either XX or XY, is made of the ___ chromosomes.
column28: The X and Y are the sex chromosomes; they determine biological sex. A common mistake is writing autosome, which is the name for pairs 1 through 22.
column29: These chromosomes decide whether a person is male or female.

column9: Where do the X and Y chromosomes go on a finished human karyotype?
column15: In the middle, next to the largest autosomes
column16: They are left off the karyotype
column17: Last, after pair 22
column28: The sex chromosomes are placed last as pair 23, after the 22 autosome pairs. They are not numbered by size like the autosomes, and they are always included because they show biological sex.
column29: The autosomes are numbered 1 to 22 first. What number is left for the sex chromosomes?

column9: When building a karyotype, which three features do you use to find each chromosome's matching partner?
column14: Color, weight, and the number of genes you can see
column15: Which parent it came from, its age, and its temperature
column16: How close it was to the other chromosome in the photo
column17: Size, centromere position, and banding pattern
column28: Homologous chromosomes are the same size, have the centromere in the same spot, and show the same banding pattern after staining. You cannot see genes or which parent a chromosome came from, and where a chromosome landed in the photo is random.
column29: Think about what you can actually see when you look at a stained chromosome under a microscope.

column9: Why are chromosomes stained before scientists make a karyotype?
column14: To kill any bacteria on the microscope slide so they don't block the chromosomes
column15: So each chromosome shows its own stripe pattern, which helps match the pairs
column16: To make the chromosomes copy themselves
column17: To turn the chromosomes into gametes
column28: Chromosomes absorb the stain unevenly, which gives each one a light-and-dark stripe pattern. Homologous chromosomes have the same pattern, so the stain is a matching tool. Stain does not copy DNA or kill bacteria.
column29: Without the stain, many chromosomes of a similar size would look alike. What does staining add?

column9: A doctor wants a karyotype of an adult patient. Which sample is most commonly used?
column15: A fingernail clipping
column16: A strand of hair cut with scissors
column17: A blood sample
column28: Karyotypes are usually made from white blood cells in a blood sample, because those cells have a nucleus and can be grown and made to divide. Nail clippings and cut hair are dead material with no living cells, and sweat has almost no cells.
column29: You need living cells that have a nucleus full of chromosomes.

column9: To make a karyotype of an unborn baby, doctors can test which sample?
column15: The father's blood
column16: Amniotic fluid from the sac around the baby
column17: The mother's hair
column28: Amniotic fluid surrounds the baby and holds cells the baby has shed, so a karyotype made from it shows the baby's chromosomes. The mother's saliva or hair and the father's blood would show the parents' chromosomes, not the baby's.
column29: Which sample comes from right around the baby instead of from a parent?

column9: Which karyotype result describes a typical male?
column15: 46,XY
column16: 47,XXY
column28: A typical male has 46 chromosomes and the sex chromosomes XY. 46,XX is a typical female, 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome, and 45,X is Turner syndrome. A common mistake is choosing 47,XXY because it has a Y; it also has an extra chromosome.
column29: Look for the typical total number AND the male sex chromosomes.

column9: What does trisomy mean?
column14: A chromosome is missing from one of the 23 pairs in the cell
column15: The cell has three complete sets of chromosomes instead of the usual two
column16: There are three copies of one chromosome instead of two
column17: A chromosome has three centromeres
column28: Tri- means three: a trisomy is three copies of one chromosome, which makes 47 in a human. Three complete sets of every chromosome is a different condition called triploidy, and a missing chromosome is a monosomy.
column29: Tri- means three. Three of what: one chromosome, or every chromosome?

column9: A karyotype shows only one chromosome 7 instead of a pair. Which term describes this?
column15: Monosomy
column16: Deletion
column17: Polyploidy
column28: Mono- means one, so having a single copy of a chromosome is a monosomy. A deletion is when only part of a chromosome is missing, and trisomy is an extra copy. Choosing deletion is the common mix-up.
column29: Is the whole chromosome gone, or just a piece of it?

column9: Down syndrome is caused by which chromosome change?
column15: Three copies of chromosome 18
column16: A missing X chromosome
column17: An extra X chromosome in a male
column28: Down syndrome is trisomy 21: three copies of chromosome 21. Trisomy 18 is Edwards syndrome, a missing X is Turner syndrome, and an extra X in a male is Klinefelter syndrome.
column29: Down syndrome is often called by a trisomy number. Which number?

column9: Which karyotype matches Turner syndrome?
column15: 45,X (one X and no second sex chromosome)
column17: 46,XY
column28: Turner syndrome is a female with only one X chromosome (written 45,X or XO). 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome and 47,XX,+21 is Down syndrome. A common mix-up is switching Turner and Klinefelter.
column29: Turner syndrome is a monosomy of the sex chromosomes.

column9: Which sex chromosomes does a person with Klinefelter syndrome have?
column15: XO
column16: XXY
column17: XYY
column28: Klinefelter syndrome is XXY, a male with an extra X (47 chromosomes total). XO is Turner syndrome, and XYY is a different extra-Y condition.
column29: Klinefelter syndrome is a male with one extra X.

column9: Edwards syndrome involves which chromosome?
column15: Chromosome 18
column16: Chromosome 21
column17: Chromosome 5
column28: Edwards syndrome is trisomy 18. Trisomy 13 is Patau syndrome, trisomy 21 is Down syndrome, and a deletion on chromosome 5 is cri-du-chat syndrome. Mixing up the trisomy numbers is the most common error.
column29: The three common trisomies are 13, 18, and 21. Down syndrome is 21. Which of the other two is Edwards?

column9: Patau syndrome is caused by trisomy ___. Type the chromosome number.
column28: Patau syndrome is trisomy 13, three copies of chromosome 13. Writing 18 (Edwards) or 21 (Down) is the common mix-up.
column29: It is the lowest-numbered of the three trisomies in the notes (13, 18, 21).

column9: Which person is most likely to have a karyotype ordered by a doctor?
column14: A teen with a sprained ankle
column15: An adult with a common cold
column16: A runner checking her heart rate
column17: A newborn with physical features of Down syndrome
column28: Karyotypes check for extra, missing, or broken chromosomes, so they are ordered when a chromosomal disorder is suspected, such as a newborn with features of Down syndrome. Injuries, infections, and heart rate have nothing to do with chromosome number.
column29: Which problem could be caused by an extra chromosome?

column9: Most trisomies, like Down syndrome, begin with a mistake during which process?
column15: Mitosis in an adult's skin cells after a sunburn
column16: Healing after a cut
column17: Meiosis, while eggs or sperm are being made
column28: Most trisomies start with nondisjunction during meiosis, which makes an egg or sperm with an extra chromosome. When that gamete is fertilized, the baby has the extra chromosome in every cell. A mistake in an adult's skin cell would not be passed to a child.
column29: The extra chromosome has to be in the baby from the very first cell. Where did that first cell's chromosomes come from?

column9: Which sex chromosome does every human egg cell carry?
column15: Y
column16: Either X or Y
column17: X
column28: A mother is XX, so every egg she makes gets an X. Only sperm can carry either an X or a Y, so choosing 'either' mixes up eggs and sperm.
column29: What sex chromosomes does the mother have to give?

column9: How many sex chromosomes are in a typical human body cell? Type a number.
column28: A typical body cell has one pair of sex chromosomes, so 2 total (XX or XY). Answering 1 confuses pairs with chromosomes, and 23 is the number of the pair, not the count.
column29: The sex chromosomes make up one pair.

column9: Make a Punnett square crossing a mother (XX) with a father (XY). What percent of the boxes are XX? Type the number only.
column28: The mother's X and X go across the top; the father's X and Y go down the side. Two boxes are XX and two are XY, so 2 out of 4 = 50%. Answering 25% means only one XX box was counted.
column29: Put the mother's two X's across the top and the father's X and Y down the side, then fill in all four boxes.

column9: Chromosome 9 is an example of which type of chromosome?
column15: Gamete
column16: Autosome
column17: Centromere
column28: Any chromosome numbered 1 through 22 is an autosome, so chromosome 9 is an autosome. Only X and Y are sex chromosomes. A gamete is a whole sex cell, and a centromere is one part of a chromosome.
column29: Is 9 one of the numbered pairs or pair 23?

column9: What do the two chromosomes in a homologous pair have in common?
column14: They carry genes for the same traits in the same order
column15: They have exactly the same alleles for every gene
column16: They both came from the mother
column17: They are always different sizes
column28: Homologous chromosomes carry the same genes in the same order, so they match in size and banding. They can carry different alleles of those genes, because one came from each parent. Saying they are identical in every allele is the common mistake.
column29: Same genes does not have to mean same versions of those genes.

column9: In a human karyotype, the Y chromosome is much smaller than the X chromosome.
column28: True. The X is a medium-large chromosome, and the Y is one of the smallest. That is why pair 23 in a male does not look like a matched pair.
column29: Picture pair 23 in a male. Do the two chromosomes match in size?

column9: How many chromosomes are in a typical human sperm cell? Type a number.
column28: Sperm and eggs are haploid, with one chromosome from each pair: 23. Answering 46 gives the body-cell number; fertilization brings two sets of 23 together to make 46.
column29: A sperm has one chromosome from each pair, not both.

column9: The pinched-in point on a chromosome, used as one clue for matching pairs on a karyotype, is called the ___.
column28: The centromere is the pinched-in point of a chromosome. Where it sits (middle or near one end) helps you match homologous pairs. A common wrong answer is centriole, which is a different cell structure.
column29: The word starts with centro-, meaning center.

column9: The light and dark stripes that show up on a stained chromosome are called ___.
column20: bands|band|banding|banding pattern|banding patterns|a banding pattern|band pattern
column28: The stripes are bands, and each chromosome's banding pattern is unique. Matching banding patterns is how you tell similar-sized chromosomes apart.
column29: This word describes stripes, like a band of color.

column9: A vet's lab report for a dog's karyotype reads 78,XX. What does the number 78 tell you?
column15: The number of chromosome pairs in each of the dog's body cells
column16: The total number of chromosomes in the dog's body cells
column17: The number of genes carried on the dog's X chromosome alone
column28: The first number in karyotype notation is the total chromosome count in a body cell. Dogs have 78 chromosomes (39 pairs), and XX means the dog is female. Reading the number as pairs is the common mistake.
column29: In a human report like 46,XY, what does the 46 stand for?

column9: A karyotype has 47 chromosomes. What does that tell you right away?
column14: The person has a typical karyotype
column15: The person is male
column16: The person is missing a chromosome
column17: The person has one extra chromosome
column28: The typical human total is 46, so 47 means one extra chromosome (a trisomy). The count alone does not tell you the sex, you have to check pair 23 for that. Missing a chromosome would give 45.
column29: Compare 47 to the typical human number.

column9: Nondisjunction during meiosis can produce which kind of gametes?
column14: Gametes that have been copied by mitosis
column15: Gametes with exactly the same number as body cells
column16: Gametes with no DNA at all
column17: Gametes with one extra or one missing chromosome
column28: In nondisjunction, a chromosome pair (or sister chromatids) fails to separate, so one gamete ends up with an extra copy and another ends up missing that chromosome. The gametes still have DNA; they just have the wrong count for one chromosome.
column29: If two chromosomes that should split up both go to the same cell, what does the other cell get?

column9: The chance of a baby having Down syndrome goes up as which factor increases?
column15: The mother's age
column16: The father's height
column17: The number of times the mother has exercised
column28: The risk of Down syndrome rises with the mother's age, because nondisjunction becomes more likely in older eggs. Birth weight, height, and exercise do not change chromosome number.
column29: Eggs form before a girl is born and wait for years. What changes as they wait?

column9: Which condition is found only in females?
column15: Turner syndrome
column16: Down syndrome
column17: Edwards syndrome
column28: Turner syndrome is a single X with no Y, so the person is always female. Klinefelter syndrome is XXY, so it is always male. Down and Edwards syndromes are autosomal trisomies and can occur in either sex.
column29: Which condition has no Y chromosome at all?

column9: A boy has one X chromosome. Which parent gave it to him?
column15: Either parent
column16: Both parents
column17: His mother
column28: A boy got his Y from his father, so his X must have come from his mother. Every egg carries an X. Saying the father gave the X is the common mistake; if the father's sperm had carried an X, the baby would be a girl.
column29: Which parent gave him the Y? Then the X had to come from the other one.

column9: A girl has two X chromosomes. Where did they come from?
column15: One from her mother and one from her father
column16: Both from her father
column17: One from her mother; the other forms after birth
column28: Her mother's egg gave one X, and her father's sperm gave the other X. That X-carrying sperm is what made her a girl. Thinking both X's came from the mother is the common mistake.
column29: Every child gets one sex chromosome from each parent.

column9: Put these human chromosomes in order from largest to smallest.
column15: Chromosome 1
column16: Chromosome 13
column17: Chromosome 5
column28: Autosomes are numbered by size, so chromosome 1 is largest, then 5, then 13, then 18. A common mistake is thinking higher numbers are bigger.
column29: The numbers on a karyotype were given by size. Does pair 1 start big or small?

column9: Which of these can a karyotype NOT show?
column14: Whether there is an extra whole chromosome
column15: Whether the person is male or female
column16: Which allele for eye color the person has
column17: Whether a large piece of a chromosome is missing
column28: A karyotype shows whole chromosomes, so it can show extra or missing chromosomes, large missing pieces, and the sex chromosomes. A single gene, like an eye-color allele, is far too small to see on a karyotype. Thinking a karyotype shows individual genes is a common mistake.
column29: A karyotype is a picture of chromosomes. Can you see one gene in that picture?

column9: A couple already has three sons. The chance that their next baby is a girl is still 50%.
column28: True. Each baby's sex is decided by which sperm fertilizes the egg, and that chance is 50% X and 50% Y every time. Earlier births do not change the odds; thinking a girl is 'due' is a common mistake.
column29: Does a sperm 'know' how many sons the family already has?

column9: Karyotypes can only be made from human cells.
column28: False. Any organism whose cells have chromosomes can be karyotyped, including dogs, corn, and fruit flies. Scientists use karyotypes of animals and plants in breeding and research.
column29: Do dogs and plants have chromosomes?

column9: Dog body cells have 78 chromosomes. How many pairs would a dog karyotype show? Type a number.
column28: Each pair has 2 chromosomes, so 78 / 2 = 39 pairs. A common mistake is multiplying by 2 instead of dividing.
column29: Each pair is made of two chromosomes.

column9: Which is a disorder of the sex chromosomes rather than the autosomes?
column15: Edwards syndrome
column16: Klinefelter syndrome
column17: Patau syndrome
column28: Klinefelter syndrome (XXY) involves pair 23, the sex chromosomes. Down (21), Edwards (18), and Patau (13) are all trisomies of autosomes.
column29: Which disorder is written with X's and Y's instead of a chromosome number?

column9: Match each karyotype term to its meaning.
column14: Karyotype :: A picture of chromosomes sorted into pairs by size, centromere, and bands
column15: Autosome :: Any chromosome in pairs 1 through 22
column16: Trisomy :: Three copies of one chromosome
column17: Monosomy :: Only one copy of a chromosome
column18: Nondisjunction :: Chromosomes fail to separate when gametes are made
column28: A karyotype is the sorted picture; autosomes are pairs 1-22; trisomy is three copies and monosomy is one copy; nondisjunction is the separation mistake that causes them. Mixing up trisomy and monosomy is the most common error: tri = three, mono = one.
column29: Use the prefixes: tri- means three, mono- means one, non- means not.

column9: Match each tool or sample to what it is used for.
column14: Karyotype :: Shows whether whole chromosomes are extra, missing, or broken
column15: Pedigree :: Traces a trait through several generations of a family
column16: Punnett square :: Predicts the chances of offspring genotypes
column17: Amniotic fluid :: Provides an unborn baby's cells for testing
column28: Karyotypes show whole chromosomes; pedigrees follow a trait through a family tree; Punnett squares predict offspring chances; amniotic fluid supplies the baby's cells for a prenatal karyotype. A common mistake is thinking a karyotype can track a single-gene trait like a pedigree does.
column29: Which tool is a picture, which is a family tree, and which is a grid?

column9: A karyotype shows two copies of each autosome except chromosome 18, which has three. Pair 23 is XX. What does the karyotype show?
column15: A female with Down syndrome
column16: A female with Edwards syndrome
column17: A female with Turner syndrome
column28: Three copies of chromosome 18 is trisomy 18, Edwards syndrome, and XX means female. Down syndrome would be three copies of chromosome 21. A common mistake is checking only the extra chromosome and forgetting to read pair 23 for the sex.
column29: Do two checks: which autosome has an extra copy, and what is pair 23?

column9: A karyotype has 45 chromosomes. Pairs 1-22 are complete, and position 23 has a single X. A student says this must be a male because there is only one X. What is wrong with the student's reasoning?
column14: Nothing; one X means the person is male
column15: A person is male only if a Y is present, so this person is female
column16: The person must have an extra X chromosome that did not show up in the photo
column17: Karyotypes with 45 chromosomes cannot be read, because a pair is incomplete
column28: Maleness comes from the Y chromosome, not from having one X. With no Y, this person is female, and a single X with 45 chromosomes is Turner syndrome. Klinefelter syndrome is XXY.
column29: What chromosome does a male have that this karyotype is missing?

column9: A karyotype reads 47,XXY. What is the person's biological sex, and why?
column14: Male, because a Y chromosome is present
column15: Female, because there are two X chromosomes
column16: Female, because the X's outnumber the Y
column17: It cannot be told when there are three sex chromosomes
column28: The Y chromosome carries the gene that makes a baby develop as male, so any karyotype with a Y is male. 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome. Counting X's to decide the sex is the common mistake.
column29: Which chromosome decides male: having a Y, or having fewer X's?

column9: Put the steps for making and reading a karyotype in order.
column14: Arrange the pairs from largest to smallest, with the sex chromosomes last
column15: Collect a blood sample
column16: Stain the chromosomes and photograph them
column17: Count the chromosomes and look for anything extra or missing
column18: Cut out each chromosome and match it with its partner
column28: Collect cells, stain and photograph the chromosomes, pair them up, arrange the pairs by size, then count and look for problems. A common mistake is counting before the pairs are sorted, which makes extra or missing chromosomes easy to miss.
column29: You can't match chromosomes you haven't photographed, and you can't spot a missing partner before the pairs are lined up.

column9: Cat body cells have 38 chromosomes, including one pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY), just like humans. How many pairs of autosomes does a cat have? Type a number.
column28: 38 chromosomes / 2 = 19 pairs. One pair is the sex chromosomes, so 19 - 1 = 18 pairs of autosomes. Answering 19 forgets to remove the sex chromosome pair.
column29: Find the total number of pairs first, then take away the sex chromosome pair.

column9: A chimpanzee karyotype shows 24 pairs of chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a typical chimpanzee egg cell? Type a number.
column28: 24 pairs = 48 chromosomes in a body cell. An egg gets one chromosome from each pair, so it has 24. Answering 48 gives the body-cell number, and 12 halves the pairs instead of the chromosomes.
column29: An egg cell gets one chromosome from every pair.

column9: A student pairs chromosomes on a karyotype worksheet by matching ones that are the same shade of gray in the photo. Why is this a poor method?
column14: Different chromosomes can look the same shade, so shade can't show which ones are true partners
column15: Gray chromosomes are always sex chromosomes
column16: Shade is the only feature that matters, so it is a good method
column17: Pairs should be matched by which side of the photo they are on, since partners always sit near each other
column28: Many chromosomes can look the same shade after staining, so shade is not a reliable clue. True partners are matched by their size, centromere position, and the pattern of their bands. Where a chromosome sits in the photo is random.
column29: Could two chromosomes of very different sizes be the same shade of gray?

column9: Select every problem that a karyotype can reveal. Select all that apply.
column15: A missing X chromosome
column16: A large missing piece of chromosome 5
column17: The allele that causes sickle cell disease
column28: A karyotype shows whole chromosomes and large pieces, so it can reveal extra or missing chromosomes (21, X, Y) and large deletions. Sickle cell disease and blood type come from single genes, which are much too small to see on a karyotype. Picking those two is the common mistake.
column29: For each choice ask: is this a whole chromosome or a big piece of one, or is it a single gene?

column9: Sickle cell disease is caused by a change in one gene. Which tool would best show how it is passed down in a family?
column14: A karyotype of one family member
column15: A count of each person's chromosomes
column16: A pedigree or Punnett square
column17: A stain of the person's chromosomes
column28: A single gene is too small to see on a karyotype, and a person with sickle cell disease still has 46 normal-looking chromosomes. Pedigrees and Punnett squares track single-gene traits. Karyotypes are used for chromosome disorders, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Would one changed gene change how the chromosomes look or how many there are?

column9: A couple plans to have two children. What is the percent chance that both children are girls? Type the number only.
column28: Each child has a 1/2 chance of being a girl. Both girls = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4 = 25%. Answering 50% treats the two births as one event.
column29: Find the chance for one child, then multiply for the second child.

column9: A boy's Y chromosome was passed down from which grandparent?
column15: His father's father
column16: His father's mother
column17: His mother's mother
column28: The boy's Y came from his father, and his father's Y came from the father's father. Women do not have a Y, so neither grandmother could pass one on. Choosing the mother's father is the common mistake: the mother has no Y to pass along.
column29: Only males carry a Y. Follow it back one generation at a time.

column9: During meiosis I in a mother, chromosome pair 21 fails to separate. What chromosome numbers could her eggs have?
column15: 46 or 0
column16: 23 only
column28: A normal egg has 23. If both copies of chromosome 21 go to one egg, it has 24, and the other egg is missing chromosome 21 and has 22. The numbers 47 and 45 are zygotes after fertilization, not eggs, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Start from the normal egg number, then add one or take one away.

column9: Because of nondisjunction, a sperm cell is missing one chromosome and has only 22. It fertilizes a normal egg. How many chromosomes will the zygote have? Type a number.
column28: A normal egg has 23. 22 + 23 = 45, a monosomy. Answering 44 doubles the sperm number, and 46 forgets that the sperm was missing one.
column29: Add the sperm's chromosomes to a normal egg's chromosomes.

column9: A karyotype shows 46 chromosomes, but one chromosome 5 is clearly shorter than its partner, with its tip missing. Which condition fits?
column15: Patau syndrome
column16: Down syndrome
column17: Cri-du-chat syndrome
column28: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by a deletion (missing piece) of chromosome 5. The count stays at 46 because no whole chromosome is missing. Turner, Patau, and Down syndromes change the chromosome count.
column29: No whole chromosome is gone, but part of chromosome 5 is. Which disorder is a deletion?

column9: Why are cells for a karyotype stopped in the middle of cell division, at metaphase?
column14: The chromosomes are fully coiled, so they are thickest and easiest to see
column15: The cell has no chromosomes at that point
column16: The DNA has not been copied yet
column17: The nuclear envelope is thickest at that point, which protects the chromosomes
column28: At metaphase the chromosomes are fully condensed, so they are short, thick, and easy to photograph and match. During interphase the DNA is spread out as chromatin and individual chromosomes can't be seen. Thinking chromosomes are always visible is the common mistake.
column29: When during the cell cycle are chromosomes most tightly packed?

column9: How many autosomes (single chromosomes, not pairs) are in a typical human egg cell? Type a number.
column28: An egg has 23 chromosomes: 22 autosomes plus one X. Answering 23 counts the X as an autosome, and 44 is the number of autosomes in a body cell.
column29: An egg has one of each chromosome. Take away the sex chromosome.

column9: Match each karyotype to the person it describes.
column15: 47,XX,+21 :: Female with Down syndrome
column16: 45,X :: Female with Turner syndrome
column17: 47,XXY :: Male with Klinefelter syndrome
column28: Read the total, then the sex chromosomes, then any +number for an extra autosome: +21 is Down and +13 is Patau. A single X with no Y is a Turner female, and XXY is a Klinefelter male. A common mistake is calling 45,X male because it has no second X.
column29: Read each one left to right: total count, sex chromosomes, then any extra autosome.

column9: You are designing a karyotype to demonstrate trisomy 21 in a male. Which notation should your finished karyotype have?
column28: Trisomy 21 adds one chromosome, so the total is 47; a male is XY; and +21 shows the extra chromosome 21. 47,XX,+21 is the female version, and 45 would mean a chromosome is missing.
column29: You need three things: the right total, the male sex chromosomes, and the extra chromosome.

column9: Select every karyotype that belongs to a male. Select all that apply.
column15: 46,XY
column16: 47,XYY
column28: Any karyotype with a Y chromosome is male: 47,XXY, 46,XY, and 47,XYY. 45,X, 47,XXX, and 46,XX have no Y, so they are female. Counting X's instead of looking for a Y is the common mistake.
column29: Check each one for a single thing: is there a Y?

column9: Select every karyotype that shows a trisomy. Select all that apply.
column15: 47,XXX
column17: 46,XY
column28: A trisomy is three copies of one chromosome, so the total is 47. 47,XX,+21 and 47,XY,+13 are autosome trisomies, and 47,XXX is a trisomy of the X chromosome (three X's). 45,X is a monosomy. Missing XXX because it has no '+' sign is the common mistake.
column29: Look for a total of 47, then make sure it is three copies of one chromosome.

column9: A karyotype reads 47,XX,+13. Which describes this person?
column15: A male with Patau syndrome
column16: A female with Edwards syndrome
column17: A female with Down syndrome
column28: +13 means an extra chromosome 13, which is Patau syndrome, and XX means female. Edwards is +18 and Down is +21. Mixing up the three trisomy numbers is the common mistake.
column29: XX tells you the sex. Which syndrome matches an extra 13?

column9: Based on a Punnett square for sex, about how many of 300 babies born at a hospital would you expect to be boys? Type a number.
column28: The Punnett square gives a 50% chance of a boy, and 50% of 300 = 150. Real numbers vary a little, but 150 is the expected value. A common mistake is using 25% from a two-child problem.
column29: What fraction of the Punnett square boxes are XY?

column9: Put these events in order, from making gametes to making a karyotype of the person.
column14: A zygote forms with one set of chromosomes from each parent
column15: Meiosis makes eggs and sperm with 23 chromosomes each
column16: Mitosis copies the zygote's chromosomes into every new body cell
column17: A sperm fertilizes an egg
column18: Doctors make a karyotype from the person's white blood cells
column28: Meiosis makes gametes, fertilization joins a sperm and an egg into a zygote, and mitosis copies those chromosomes into every body cell, which is why a karyotype from blood cells shows the chromosomes the person inherited. A common mistake is putting mitosis before fertilization.
column29: Gametes come first. What has to happen before there is a zygote to copy?

column9: A newborn is diagnosed with Edwards syndrome. How many chromosomes would her karyotype show? Type a number.
column28: Edwards syndrome is trisomy 18: one extra copy of chromosome 18, so 46 + 1 = 47. Answering 49 adds three chromosomes instead of one; three copies means just one extra.
column29: Edwards syndrome is a trisomy. How many extra chromosomes does a trisomy add?

column9: A student finishes a typical human karyotype and writes, "This person has 23 chromosomes." What mistake did the student make?
column14: The student counted pairs instead of single chromosomes
column15: The student forgot to count the autosomes
column16: There is no mistake
column17: The student counted only the sex chromosomes
column28: A karyotype lines chromosomes up in pairs, so it is easy to count 23 pairs and forget that each pair has two chromosomes. The total for a typical person is twice the number of pairs.
column29: How many chromosomes are in each spot on the karyotype?

column9: A woman's karyotype is 46,XX. How many X chromosomes are in each of her egg cells? Type a number.
column28: During meiosis her two X chromosomes separate, so each egg gets one X. Answering 2 forgets that gametes get only one chromosome from each pair.
column29: Gametes get one chromosome from each pair, and her X's are a pair.

column9: A student cuts out a full set of chromosomes from a typical person and pairs them. Two chromosomes are left that do not match each other in size or banding. What are they most likely, and what does that show?
column14: Two broken autosomes, which shows a deletion
column15: An X and a Y, which shows the person is male
column16: Two X chromosomes, which shows the person is female
column17: Two copies of chromosome 21, which shows Down syndrome
column28: Every autosome has a matching partner, and two X's would match each other. The only typical pair that does not match is X and Y, so the person is male. Calling it a deletion is the common mistake; X and Y are naturally different.
column29: In a typical person, which pair is the only one whose two members look different?

column9: In a karyotype photo, each chromosome looks like an X shape. Why?
column14: Every chromosome is an X chromosome
column15: Two homologous chromosomes, one from each parent, are stuck together where they cross in the middle
column16: Each chromosome was copied before division, so it is two sister chromatids joined at the centromere
column17: The stain bends the chromosome into an X
column28: The DNA was copied during interphase, so in metaphase each chromosome is two identical sister chromatids held at the centromere. That X shape has nothing to do with the X sex chromosome, and it is not two homologous chromosomes stuck together, which are common mix-ups.
column29: What happened to the DNA during interphase, before the cell started dividing?

column9: How many autosomes (single chromosomes, not pairs) are in a typical human body cell? Type a number.
column28: There are 22 pairs of autosomes, and 22 x 2 = 44. The other 2 chromosomes are the sex chromosomes. Answering 22 counts pairs, and 46 includes the sex chromosomes.
column29: Count the autosome pairs, then count how many chromosomes are in those pairs.

column9: Half of a man's sperm carry an X chromosome and half carry a Y. Why?
column14: During meiosis his X and Y separate, so each sperm gets one of them
column15: His body makes X sperm on some days and Y sperm on others, depending on hormones
column16: The Y chromosome copies itself into an X
column17: Sperm get their sex chromosome from the egg
column28: A man is XY. In meiosis the X and Y separate into different cells, so half the sperm get the X and half get the Y. That is why a child's sex depends on the sperm. Sperm do not get anything from the egg before fertilization.
column29: He has one X and one Y, and each sperm gets one chromosome from each pair.

column9: Doctors use white blood cells, not red blood cells, to make a karyotype from a blood sample. Why?
column14: Red blood cells have too many chromosomes to count
column15: White blood cells have more chromosomes than other cells, so they are easier to count
column16: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, so they have no chromosomes
column17: Red blood cells contain only X chromosomes
column28: Mature human red blood cells lose their nucleus as they develop, so they have no chromosomes to photograph. White blood cells keep their nucleus and can be made to divide. Every body cell with a nucleus has the same 46 chromosomes, so white blood cells do not have 'more.'
column29: Where in a cell are the chromosomes kept? Do red blood cells have that part?

column9: A person can live with the karyotype 45,X, but an embryo with a Y and no X does not survive. What best explains this?
column14: The Y chromosome is larger than the X and crowds out the other chromosomes
column15: The X carries many genes needed for life that the Y does not have
column16: The Y chromosome is an autosome
column17: Embryos need two Y chromosomes to survive
column28: The X is a large chromosome with many genes every cell needs, while the small Y carries few genes, mostly for male development. Without any X, those needed genes are missing. The Y is actually much smaller than the X, so saying it is larger is a mistake.
column29: Think about the size of the X and the Y and how many genes each can hold.

column9: Karyotype A is 47,XY,+21 and karyotype B is 47,XXY. Both have 47 chromosomes. Where is the extra chromosome on each karyotype?
column14: A: a third chromosome at pair 21; B: an extra X at pair 23
column15: Both: a third chromosome at pair 21
column16: A: an extra X at pair 23; B: a third chromosome at pair 21
column17: Both: an extra chromosome at pair 23
column28: Karyotype A (Down syndrome) has +21, an extra autosome, so pair 21 has three copies. Karyotype B (Klinefelter syndrome) is XXY, so the extra chromosome is an X at pair 23. The same total count can come from different extra chromosomes, so you always have to find where the extra one is.
column29: Read each notation: a +number means an extra autosome, and extra letters mean an extra sex chromosome.

column9: A woman's karyotype shows 46 chromosomes, XX, with all pairs matching. Her family has a history of cystic fibrosis, a single-gene disorder. What can you conclude?
column14: She does not carry the cystic fibrosis allele, because all 46 of her chromosomes are normal and in matching pairs
column15: She has cystic fibrosis
column16: The karyotype rules out a chromosome-number problem but can't show if she carries the cystic fibrosis allele
column17: The karyotype shows she is male
column28: A normal karyotype means no extra, missing, or large broken chromosomes. Cystic fibrosis comes from one gene, which is far too small to see, so the karyotype says nothing about it. A pedigree or a genetic test is needed. Assuming a normal karyotype means 'no genetic disorders' is the common mistake.
column29: Can a single gene be seen on a karyotype?

column9: Nondisjunction happens during mitosis in one skin cell on an adult's arm. Could this extra chromosome be passed to the adult's future children?
column14: Yes, every mistake in any cell is passed to children, no matter where it happens
column15: Yes, but only to sons
column16: No, because skin cells carry only autosomes and no sex chromosomes at all
column17: No, because only chromosomes in eggs or sperm are passed to children
column28: Children inherit only the chromosomes in the egg and sperm, which are made by meiosis. A mistake in a skin cell affects only that cell and the cells it makes. Skin cells do have sex chromosomes too, so that reason is wrong.
column29: Which cells actually carry chromosomes from a parent to a child?

column9: One chromosome pair fails to separate during meiosis I, and meiosis II goes normally. Out of the 4 gametes made, how many have the wrong number of chromosomes? Type a number.
column28: If the pair fails to separate in meiosis I, one cell gets both copies and the other gets none. Meiosis II splits each of those cells, making 2 gametes with an extra chromosome and 2 gametes missing it, so all 4 are abnormal. Answering 2 matches a mistake in meiosis II, not meiosis I.
column29: Follow both cells from meiosis I. Does either one have a normal set going into meiosis II?

column9: Chimpanzee body cells have 48 chromosomes. Because of nondisjunction, a chimp egg has one extra chromosome. It is fertilized by a normal chimp sperm. How many chromosomes does the zygote have? Type a number.
column28: A normal chimp gamete has 48 / 2 = 24. The egg has 24 + 1 = 25, and the sperm has 24, so the zygote has 25 + 24 = 49. Answering 47 uses human numbers.
column29: Find a normal chimp gamete number first, then adjust the egg.

column9: A girl has Turner syndrome (45,X). Which parent's gamete could have been missing a sex chromosome?
column15: Only the father's sperm
column16: Either parent's gamete
column17: Neither; Turner syndrome starts after birth
column28: An egg with no X plus an X-carrying sperm gives 45,X, and so does a normal X egg plus a sperm with no sex chromosome. Either parent's nondisjunction can cause it. A common mistake is thinking it must be the mother because the child is a girl.
column29: Try both cases: an egg with no sex chromosome, and a sperm with no sex chromosome. What does each make?

column9: Select every egg + sperm combination that would produce a zygote with Klinefelter syndrome (XXY). Select all that apply.
column14: An XX egg + a Y sperm
column15: An X egg + an XY sperm
column16: An X egg + an X sperm
column17: An egg with no X + an XY sperm
column18: An XX egg + an X sperm
column28: Add the sex chromosomes from each gamete: XX + Y = XXY and X + XY = XXY. X + X = XX (typical female), no X + XY = XY (typical male), and XX + X = XXX. Missing the second combination is common; nondisjunction in the father can cause Klinefelter too.
column29: Add up the sex chromosomes from the egg and the sperm for each choice.

column9: A boy has the karyotype 47,XYY. Which parent's gamete had the extra Y?
column14: The father's, because only he has a Y to pass on
column15: The mother's, because eggs can carry a Y
column16: Either parent's
column17: Neither; the Y copied itself after fertilization
column28: Mothers are XX and have no Y to give, so a YY sperm from the father must have caused it, most likely from nondisjunction in meiosis II. Eggs never carry a Y.
column29: Which parent has a Y chromosome at all?

column9: A couple plans to have three children. What is the percent chance that all three are girls? Type the number only.
column28: Each birth is a separate 1/2 chance: 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8 = 12.5%. A common mistake is adding the chances or answering 33%, as if each of three outcomes were equally likely.
column29: Multiply the chance for one girl by itself once for each child.

column9: A couple plans to have two children. What is the percent chance that at least one of them is a girl? Type the number only.
column28: The only way to have no girls is boy-boy, which is 1/2 x 1/2 = 25%. Every other outcome has at least one girl, so 100% - 25% = 75%. Answering 50% looks at only one child.
column29: It is easier to find the chance of NO girls first.

column9: A couple has two children. What is the percent chance that they have exactly one boy and one girl, in either order? Type the number only.
column28: The four equally likely outcomes are boy-boy, boy-girl, girl-boy, and girl-girl. Two of the four have one of each, so 2/4 = 50%. Answering 25% counts only one order.
column29: List all four possible birth orders for two children.

column9: Put these events in order to show how a child can end up with Down syndrome.
column15: Chromosome pair 21 fails to separate during meiosis in the mother
column16: Mitosis copies all 47 chromosomes into every body cell
column17: A normal sperm with 23 chromosomes fertilizes the egg
column19: A karyotype of the child shows three copies of chromosome 21
column28: Nondisjunction in meiosis makes an egg with 24 chromosomes; a normal sperm adds 23, making a 47-chromosome zygote; mitosis copies those 47 into every cell, so a karyotype from any body cell shows three copies of 21. A common mistake is placing mitosis before fertilization.
column29: Start with the mistake that makes the egg, and end with what the doctor sees.

column9: A karyotype from a miscarried embryo shows 69 chromosomes, with three copies of every chromosome. Which describes it?
column14: Triploidy: three full sets of chromosomes instead of two
column15: Trisomy 21
column16: Monosomy
column17: A typical karyotype
column28: 69 = 3 x 23, so there are three full sets of chromosomes. This is triploidy. A trisomy is only one chromosome with three copies (47 in humans), so calling this a trisomy is the common mistake.
column29: Divide 69 by the number of chromosomes in one set.

column9: A karyotype has 47 chromosomes, and pair 23 is XY. What else must you check before you can name the disorder?
column14: Which autosome pair has three copies
column15: Nothing; it must be Klinefelter syndrome
column16: The person's blood type
column17: Whether the person is male
column28: 47 means one extra chromosome, and XY is the typical male pair, so the extra must be an autosome. You need to find which pair has three copies: 21 (Down), 18 (Edwards), or 13 (Patau). It is not Klinefelter, because that needs XXY.
column29: If pair 23 is a normal XY, where must the extra chromosome be?

column9: A student designs a karyotype to show a trisomy of chromosome 8 in a male. She draws three copies of chromosome 8, two copies of every other autosome, and an X and a Y, then labels it 46,XY,+8. What is wrong?
column15: Chromosome 8 should have only one copy
column16: Nothing is wrong
column17: The total should be 47, not 46
column28: A trisomy adds one chromosome to the typical 46, so the label should read 47,XY,+8. The drawing is correct; only the count is wrong. Forgetting to change the total when adding the extra chromosome is a common design error.
column29: Count: 22 autosome pairs, one with an extra copy, plus two sex chromosomes.

column9: A woman got one of her X chromosomes from her father. Which of her father's parents gave him that X?
column15: Her father's mother
column16: Either of her father's parents
column17: Her mother's mother
column28: Her father is XY. He got his Y from his own father, so his only X came from his mother. That is the X he passed to his daughter. Choosing the father's father is the common mistake: a man gives his sons a Y, not an X.
column29: What did her father get from his own father: an X or a Y?

column9: A father has an unusual banding pattern on his X chromosome. Which of his children will inherit that X?
column14: All of his sons and none of his daughters
column15: All of his daughters and none of his sons
column16: Half of his daughters and half of his sons
column17: All of his children
column28: A father has only one X. Every daughter gets his X (that is what makes her XX), and every son gets his Y instead. So all daughters and no sons inherit it. Saying half of the daughters is the common mistake; a father has no second X to give.
column29: What does a father give a daughter, and what does he give a son?

column9: A mother has an unusual banding pattern on one of her two X chromosomes. What is the chance that any one child inherits that X?
column14: 100% of her sons and 0% of her daughters
column15: 25% for each child
column16: 50% for each child, son or daughter
column17: 0%, because only fathers pass on X chromosomes
column28: Every child gets one of the mother's two X's, chosen at random in meiosis, so each child has a 50% chance of getting the unusual one, whether a son or a daughter. Thinking sons always get it confuses this with how a father's single X is passed.
column29: She has two X's and each egg gets one. Does the baby's sex change which X is in the egg?

column9: Why do identical twins have matching karyotypes?
column15: They came from two eggs fertilized by two sperm at the same time, so they match exactly
column16: They both came from the same zygote, and mitosis copied the same chromosomes into both
column17: Their parents had matching karyotypes
column28: Identical twins form when one zygote splits, so both start with the same chromosomes, and mitosis copies those into every cell. Two eggs and two sperm make fraternal twins, whose karyotypes can differ, for example one XX and one XY.
column29: How many zygotes do identical twins come from?

column9: A genetic counselor has four karyotypes: 46,XX; 47,XX,+21; 45,X; and 47,XXY. Select every karyotype with a sex chromosome abnormality. Select all that apply.
column17: 47,XXY
column28: 45,X (Turner) is missing a sex chromosome and 47,XXY (Klinefelter) has an extra one. 47,XX,+21 is abnormal, but the extra chromosome is an autosome (21), and 46,XX is typical. Picking 47,XX,+21 just because it has 47 is the common mistake.
column29: For each karyotype, look only at the X's and Y's. Are there exactly two?

column9: Some people with Down syndrome have three copies of chromosome 21 in only some of their cells. Which event best explains this?
column14: Nondisjunction in the mother's egg before fertilization
column15: Nondisjunction in the father's sperm before fertilization, so the zygote got an extra 21
column16: Nondisjunction during mitosis in the early embryo, after fertilization
column17: An extra chromosome caught from a sibling
column28: If the egg or sperm had the extra 21, the zygote would have it and every cell would too. Only some cells being affected means the mistake happened in mitosis after the zygote formed, so only the cells descended from that one cell carry the extra chromosome. Blaming the egg is the common mistake.
column29: If the extra chromosome were there from the first cell, how many cells would have it?

column9: A horse has 64 chromosomes and a donkey has 62. A mule is the offspring of a horse egg and a donkey sperm. How many chromosomes does a mule have? Type a number.
column28: The horse egg has 64 / 2 = 32 and the donkey sperm has 62 / 2 = 31, so the mule has 32 + 31 = 63. Adding the full body-cell numbers to get 126 is the common error; each parent passes on only half.
column29: Each parent gives a gamete with half its body-cell number.

column9: You are designing a poster to show that Down syndrome can come from either parent. Which pair of gamete examples should you draw?
column14: An egg with two copies of chromosome 21 + a normal sperm, and a normal egg + a sperm with two copies of chromosome 21
column15: Only an egg with two copies of chromosome 21 + a normal sperm
column16: An egg missing chromosome 21 + a normal sperm
column17: Two normal eggs fertilized by one sperm
column28: Down syndrome needs one gamete with an extra chromosome 21. That extra copy can come from the egg or the sperm, so showing both cases demonstrates that either parent can contribute it. An egg missing chromosome 21 would cause a monosomy, not Down syndrome.
column29: To show 'either parent,' your poster needs one example for each parent.
